claim: Neuroeconomic theories of decision making suggest that value-based decisions can be captured by a process involving several distinct computations, including both attribute valuation and evidence accumulation.
source: Neuroeconomic theories of decision making suggest that value-based decisions can be captured by a process involving several distinct computations, including both attribute valuation and evidence accumulation (EA; Rangel et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rangel et al., 2008

claim: Attempts to regulate dietary behaviour may operate in part by altering the weights given to specific attributes during food choice.
source: Based on this model of choice, recent work has argued that attempts to regulate dietary behaviour may operate in part by altering the weights given to specific attributes during food choice (Hutcherson et al., 2012; Sullivan et al., 2015; Tusche and Hutcherson, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hutcherson et al., 2012; Sullivan et al., 2015; Tusche and Hutcherson, 2018

claim: Decrements in the power of alpha (9–12 Hz) and theta (4–8 Hz) oscillations correlate with the predicted build-up of evidence in perceptual decision-making.
source: For example, in the perceptual decision-making domain, electroencephalogram (EEG) studies have shown that decrements in the power of alpha (9–12 Hz) and theta (4–8 Hz) oscillations correlate with the predicted build-up of evidence (van Vugt et al., 2012; Werkle-Bergner et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Vugt et al., 2012; Werkle-Bergner et al., 2014

claim: The P300 component elicited by oddball stimuli in auditory and visual paradigms satisfies the characteristics of an evidence accumulation signal.
source: Analyses of event-related potentials (ERPs) also show that the P300 component elicited by oddball stimuli in auditory and visual paradigms satisfies the characteristics of an EA signal (decision variable) (O'Connell et al., 2012; Twomey et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Connell et al., 2012; Twomey et al., 2015

claim: Model predictions about the temporal dynamics of evidence accumulation during decisions correlate with both parietal and frontal theta and alpha in value-based decision-making.
source: Parallel to this, in the value-based decision-making domain, EEG and MEG studies have found that model predictions about the temporal dynamics of EA during decisions correlate with both parietal and frontal theta and alpha (Hunt et al., 2012), and with beta (18–20 Hz) and gamma (40–80 Hz) oscillations (Polanía et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hunt et al., 2012 and Polanía et al., 2014

claim: Self-regulation during decision making modifies choices by changing the influence of attributes on behaviour.
source: Although considerable evidence suggests that self-regulation during decision making modifies choices by changing the influence of attributes on behaviour (Hare et al., 2009; Hare et al., 2011; Hutcherson et al., 2012; Sullivan et al., 2015; Tusche and Hutcherson, 2018), it is unclear how such changes are accomplished neurally.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hare et al., 2009; Hare et al., 2011; Hutcherson et al., 2012; Sullivan et al., 2015; Tusche and Hutcherson, 2018

claim: When instructed to attend to food healthiness, the amplitude of a fronto-central ERP component around 300–500 ms post-food stimulus correlated more strongly with food healthiness.
source: For example, some research suggests that when instructed to attend to food healthiness, the amplitude of a fronto-central ERP component around 300–500 ms post-food stimulus correlated more strongly with food healthiness (Harris et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harris et al., 2013

claim: While regulation reduced behavioural sensitivity to tastiness considerations, ERP amplitude in the same time window correlated with tastiness regardless of regulatory effort.
source: Moreover, while regulation reduced behavioural sensitivity to tastiness considerations, ERP amplitude in the same time window correlated with tastiness regardless of regulatory effort (Harris et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harris et al., 2013

claim: Subjects accepted foods less often in DECREASE compared to both NATURAL and HEALTH conditions.
source: As expected, subjects accepted foods less often in DECREASE compared to both NATURAL (t(49) = −4.0, p<0.001) and HEALTH (t(49) = −3.9, p<0.001), which did not differ from each other (p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data showing significant differences in acceptance rates

claim: Response times were affected by regulation, with subjects being faster in the NATURAL condition compared to both HEALTH and DECREASE conditions.
source: Response times were also affected by regulation (F(2,98) = 7.33, p=0.004). Subjects were faster in the NATURAL compared to both HEALTH (t(49) = −5.7, p<0.001) and DECREASE (t(49) = −2.6, p=0.01) which were not significantly different from each other (p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data showing significant differences in response times

claim: Regulation had a significant effect on the weight given to tastiness.
source: As expected, we found that regulation had a significant effect on the weight given to tastiness (wtastiness: F(2,98) = 33.17, p<0.001)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of drift-diffusion model parameters

claim: Weight on tastiness decreased to a similar extent in HEALTH and DECREASE compared to NATURAL.
source: Post-hoc paired t-tests showed that weight on tastiness decreased to a similar extent in HEALTH (t (49) = −7.42, p<0.001) and DECREASE (t (49) = −6.18, p<0.001) compared to NATURAL.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of drift-diffusion model parameters

claim: The weight on healthiness significantly increased in both HEALTH and DECREASE compared to NATURAL.
source: By contrast, while the weight on healthiness (whealthiness) significantly increased in both HEALTH and DECREASE compared to NATURAL (HEALTH: t (49) = 9.38, p<0.001; DECREASE: t(49) = 3.56, p<0.001), it was significantly larger in HEALTH compared to DECREASE (t(49) = 7.12, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of drift-diffusion model parameters

claim: The value constant was more negative in DECREASE compared to NATURAL and HEALTH.
source: In addition, the value constant (ValConst) was more negative in DECREASE compared to NATURAL (t(49) = −4.11, p<0.001) and HEALTH (t(49) = −6.09, p<0.001), and more negative in NATURAL compared to HEALTH (t(49) = −2.38, p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of drift-diffusion model parameters

claim: Both regulatory strategies decreased the influence of tastiness on choice, while HEALTH focus specifically increased the influence of healthiness, and DECREASE resulted in a decrease in value that is non-specific to tastiness or healthiness.
source: Thus, while both strategies decreased the influence of tastiness on choice, HEALTH focus specifically increased the influence of healthiness, and DECREASE resulted in a decrease in value that is non-specific to tastiness or healthiness.
evidence: Inference drawn from the pattern of results in drift-diffusion model parameters

claim: Regulation changed the decision threshold and non-decision time.
source: In particular, it changed the decision threshold (trs: F(2,98) = 25.45, p<0.001) and non-decision time (ndt: F(2,98) = 4.69, p=0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of drift-diffusion model parameters

claim: There was little evidence that regulation affected starting point biases.
source: Notably, we found little evidence that regulation affected starting point biases (spbias: p>0.05), suggesting that most of the effects of regulation occurred during post-stimulus processing rather than in pre-stimulus preparation.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of drift-diffusion model parameters showing non-significant effects

claim: Decision threshold was higher in DECREASE compared to NATURAL and HEALTH, and in HEALTH compared to NATURAL.
source: Post-hoc paired t-tests on significant effects showed that decision threshold was higher in DECREASE compared to NATURAL (t(49) = 6.0, p<0.001) and HEALTH (t(49) = 3.67, p<0.001) and in HEALTH compared to NATURAL (t(49) = 4.87, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of drift-diffusion model parameters

claim: Non-decision time was shorter in DECREASE compared to NATURAL and HEALTH but was not different in HEALTH compared to NATURAL.
source: Non-decision time was also shorter in DECREASE compared to NATURAL (t(49) = −2.32, p=0.02) and HEALTH (t(49) = −2.72, p=0.009) but was not different in HEALTH compared to NATURAL (p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of drift-diffusion model parameters

claim: The average association between food tastiness ratings and the simulated taste attribute signal reached a maximum at 516 ms, significantly earlier than the corresponding peak of average association between tastiness ratings and the EA signal at 630 ms.
source: Across the three conditions, the average association between food tastiness ratings and the simulated taste attribute signal (btastiness taste-AC) reached a maximum at 516 ms, significantly earlier than the corresponding peak of average association between tastiness ratings and the EA signal (btastiness taste-EA) at 630 ms (t(49) = −23.64, p<0.001; Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of model simulations shown in Figure 2c

claim: The average association between food healthiness ratings and the healthiness attribute signal reached a maximum at 568 ms, significantly earlier than the peak of average contribution of food healthiness to the EA signal at 662 ms.
source: Similarly, the average association between food healthiness ratings and the healthiness attribute signal (bhealthiness health-AC) reached a maximum at 568 ms, significantly earlier than the peak of average contribution of food healthiness to the EA signal (bhealthiness health-EA) at 662 ms (t(49) = −7.07, p<0.001; Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of model simulations shown in Figure 2c

claim: Signals related to attribute representations would be expected to peak around 516–570 ms, while signals related to EA would be expected to peak later, around 630–660 ms.
source: These differences in the time course of model simulations suggest that signals related to attribute representations would be expected to peak around 516–570 ms, while signals related to EA would be expected to peak later, around 630–660 ms.
evidence: Inference drawn from the timing differences observed in model simulations

claim: ERPs in fronto-central channels were correlated with tastiness in the NATURAL condition.
source: Based on our significance criteria (see Materials and methods for details), we found that ERPs in fronto-central (t(49) = 3.45, p=0.004) channels were correlated with tastiness in the NATURAL condition.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of ERP data

claim: The ERP-correlate of tastiness showed no significant differentiation between NATURAL and regulated conditions.
source: However, this effect showed no significant differentiation between NATURAL and regulated conditions (p>0.05; but see Figure 3c for other differences in the scalp maps across NATURAL and DECREASE).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing non-significant differences, with reference to Figure 3c

claim: The time course of the ERP-correlate of tastiness was closely predicted by the simulated influence of tastiness on the taste-AC signals.
source: The time course of the ERP-correlate of tastiness was closely predicted by the simulated influence of tastiness on the taste-AC signals (r = 0.89, p<0.001) and, somewhat less clearly but still significantly, the taste-EA signal (r = 0.77, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between ERP data and model simulations

claim: The ERP-correlate of tastiness was a significantly closer match for the taste-AC than the taste-EA signal.
source: It was also a significantly closer match for the taste-AC than the taste-EA signal (z = 2.55, p=0.005; Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of correlations, shown in Figure 3b

claim: The magnitude of the ERP-correlate of tastiness was not correlated with weight on taste in the NATURAL condition or behavioural regulation across subjects.
source: The magnitude of the ERP-correlate of tastiness was not correlated with weight on taste in the NATURAL condition or behavioural regulation (i.e. the difference in the weight on taste between regulation conditions) across subjects.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing non-significant relationships

claim: Trial-by-trial ERPs in the HEALTH condition were correlated significantly with healthiness ~200–400 ms post-food in occipital channels.
source: Because we failed to find ERP signals for healthiness that matched our model-predicted time course, we also conducted an exploratory (i.e. not model-based) analysis of ERPs, which revealed that trial-by-trial ERPs in the HEALTH condition were correlated significantly with healthiness ~200–400 ms post-food in occipital channels (t(49) = 3.12, p=0.007; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by exploratory statistical analysis of ERP data, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a

claim: The early ERP signature of healthiness did not correlate with the behavioural increase in healthiness weight across subjects.
source: However, this early ERP signature of healthiness did not correlate with the behavioural increase in healthiness weight across subjects.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing non-significant relationships

claim: In the NATURAL condition, there was a significant change in alpha power over left-frontal and right parietal-occipital channels that negatively correlated with tastiness ratings from 500 to 1000 ms after presentation of food.
source: In particular, in the NATURAL condition, we found a significant change in alpha power over left-frontal and right parietal-occipital channels (Figure 4c, top left) that negatively correlated with tastiness ratings from 500 to 1000 ms after presentation of food (t(49) = −3.78, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of alpha power data, shown in Figure 4c

claim: Alpha power during the two regulation conditions (HEALTH and DECREASE) was not significantly associated with tastiness.
source: By contrast, alpha power during the two regulation conditions (HEALTH and DECREASE) was not significantly associated with tastiness.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing non-significant associations

claim: The difference in correlation between tastiness and alpha power in the window from 500 to 1000 ms was significant for the contrast of DECREASE vs. NATURAL and marginally significant for HEALTH vs. NATURAL.
source: The difference in correlation between tastiness and alpha power in the window from 500 to 1000 ms was significant for the contrast of DECREASE vs. NATURAL (t (49) = 2.40, p=0.02) and marginally significant for HEALTH vs. NATURAL (t (49) = 2.01, p=0.05; Figure 4c, bottom).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of alpha power differences, shown in Figure 4c

claim: Changes in the alpha-correlate of tastiness predicted individual differences in successful down-regulation of tastiness influence.
source: As hypothesized, we found a correlation between the decrease in the weight on tastiness (Δwtastiness) and the decrease in the alpha-correlate of tastiness ~500–1000 ms post-food, both for the comparison of DECREASE vs. NATURAL (Pearson r = −0.28, p=0.05) and the comparison of HEALTH vs. NATURAL (Pearson r = −0.29, p=0.04) (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between alpha power changes and model parameter changes, shown in Figure 4d

claim: The alpha-correlate of tastiness was predicted closely by taste-EA but not taste-AC.
source: Importantly, we found that the alpha-correlate of tastiness was predicted closely by taste-EA (ralpha-EA = −0.90, p<0.001) but not taste-AC (ralpha-tastiness = −0.70, p>0.05), with the taste-EA signal showing a more precise relationship compared to the taste-AC signal across time (z = 4.09, p<0.001; Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between alpha power and model simulations, shown in Figure 4e

claim: Regulation may operate in part by altering alpha frequency representations of tastiness attributes, and this modulation might occur in relationship to evidence accumulation rather than attribute construction.
source: These results suggest that regulation may operate in part by altering alpha frequency representations of tastiness attributes, and that this modulation might occur in relationship to EA rather than attribute construction.
evidence: Inference drawn from the pattern of correlations between alpha power and model-predicted signals

claim: Alpha signal was sensitive to tastiness for different durations on trials where the participant responded quickly compared to trials where they responded slowly.
source: Follow-up tests confirmed this hypothesis: we found that alpha signal was sensitive to tastiness for different durations on trials where the participant responded quickly compared to trials where they responded slowly (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: Supported by analysis of alpha power in fast vs. slow trials, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b

claim: Alpha signals at taste-sensitive channels showed a build-up of correlation with tastiness in NATURAL trials that peaked just before the time of response both when decisions were made quickly and when they were made slowly.
source: As expected, we found that alpha signals at taste-sensitive channels (Figure 4c, top left) showed a build-up of correlation with tastiness in NATURAL trials that peaked just before the time of response both when decisions were made quickly and when they were made slowly (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c, d).
evidence: Supported by response-locked analysis of alpha power, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c, d

claim: There was an additional significant correlation with healthiness in taste-sensitive channels prior to the response on slow trials in the NATURAL condition, but not on the fast trials.
source: Intriguingly, this analysis also revealed an additional significant correlation with healthiness in taste-sensitive channels prior to the response on slow trials in the NATURAL condition, but not on the fast trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 3e, f).
evidence: Supported by response-locked analysis of alpha power in fast vs. slow trials, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3e, f

claim: Raw alpha signals in taste-sensitive regions did build gradually, peaking in the time before response, but they did not always reach a fully clear and consistent value.
source: Although we found that raw alpha signals in this region did build gradually, peaking in the time before response (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), they did not always reach a fully clear and consistent value, as might be predicted if these signals provided the final trigger for the motor response.
evidence: Supported by analysis of raw alpha power, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The alpha-correlate of tastiness shows patterns consistent with some form of evidence accumulation, but may represent an intermediate stage of EA based on value that is then passed on to other mechanisms that accumulate evidence for a particular motor response.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that, while the alpha-correlate of tastiness shows patterns consistent with some form of EA, it may represent an intermediate stage of EA based on value that is then passed on to other mechanisms that accumulate evidence for a particular motor response.
evidence: Inference drawn from the pattern of alpha power results

claim: In the HEALTH condition, alpha power in frontal and parietal-occipital channels was negatively correlated with healthiness from ~500–1000 ms after presentation of food.
source: Notably, in the HEALTH condition, we again found significant effects restricted to alpha power in frontal and parietal-occipital channels (Figure 4b). Alpha power in these channels was negatively correlated with healthiness from ~500–1000 ms after presentation of food (t(49) = −2.96, p=0.005; alpha-correlate of healthiness; Figure 4c, top-right).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of alpha power data, shown in Figure 4b and 4c

claim: The timing of the alpha-correlate of healthiness correlated with the predicted time course of the health-EA signal and, less so, to the health-AC signals.
source: The timing of this signal correlated with the predicted time course of the health-EA signal (ralpha-EA = −0.95, p<0.001) and, less so, to the health-AC signals (ralpha-healthiness = −0.76, p=0.02) signals.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between alpha power and model simulations

claim: The time course of the alpha-correlate of healthiness was significantly more strongly correlated with the health-EA signal than the health-AC signal.
source: The time course was significantly more strongly correlated with the health-EA signal than the health-AC signal (z = 4.17, p<0.001; Figure 4f).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of correlations, shown in Figure 4f

claim: Alpha power during the NATURAL and DECREASE conditions was not significantly associated with healthiness.
source: As might be expected from model predictions, alpha power during the NATURAL and DECREASE conditions was not significantly associated with healthiness, although the contrast of average bhealthiness for alpha power between HEALTH and DECREASE or NATURAL in these channels ~500–1000 ms post-food failed to reach significance.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing non-significant associations

claim: There was no evidence that the differences in alpha-healthiness correlate across conditions correlated with individual differences in the change in model parameters for the healthiness weight.
source: Unlike the alpha-tastiness correlate, we found no evidence that the differences in alpha-healthiness correlate across conditions correlated with individual differences in the change in model parameters for the healthiness weight.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing non-significant relationships

claim: Theta power at channels over occipital and frontal areas was positively correlated with tastiness early in the trial (200–500 ms) in both HEALTH and DECREASE conditions independently.
source: Strikingly, and in contrast to alpha power, which tracks tastiness in the NATURAL condition but not regulation conditions, we found a single pattern matching our significance criterion: theta power at channels over occipital and frontal areas was positively correlated with tastiness early in the trial (200–500 ms) in both HEALTH (t(49) = 3.46, p=0.005; Figure 5a, b, top left) and DECREASE (t(49) = 2.8, p=0.01; Figure 5a, b, top-right) conditions independently.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of theta power data, shown in Figure 5a and 5b

claim: The theta-correlate of tastiness was larger compared to NATURAL in both HEALTH and DECREASE.
source: This effect was also larger compared to NATURAL in both HEALTH (t(49) = 2.90, p=0.009; occipital channels) and DECREASE (t(49) = 2.28, p=0.03; occipital and left central channels) (Figure 5b, bottom).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of theta power differences, shown in Figure 5b

claim: The theta-correlate of tastiness might represent a 'control' process responsible for reducing the influence of tastiness attribute representations on the evidence accumulation process.
source: Given the early appearance of this signal compared to the alpha-correlate of tastiness, we speculated that it might represent a 'control' process, rather than a representation of the tastiness attribute per se. This control process might be responsible for reducing the influence of tastiness attribute representations (which we observed in ERP signals) on the EA process (observed in alpha oscillations).
evidence: Speculation based on the timing and pattern of theta power results

claim: Subjects with greater increases in the theta-correlate of tastiness between 200 and 500 ms showed greater decreases in the weight on tastiness.
source: We found that subjects with greater increases in the theta-correlate of tastiness between 200 and 500 ms showed greater decreases in the weight on tastiness (Δwtastiness), and this was independently true for the contrast of both HEALTH (Pearson r = –0.36, p=0.01) and DECREASE (Pearson r = –0.29, p=0.04) vs. NATURAL (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between theta power changes and model parameter changes, shown in Figure 5c

claim: Changes in the alpha- and theta-correlates of tastiness in DECREASE vs. NATURAL were correlated across subjects.
source: Moreover, changes in the alpha- and theta-correlates of tastiness in DECREASE vs. NATURAL were correlated across subjects (Pearson r = 0.43, p<0.001; Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between alpha and theta power changes, shown in Figure 5d

claim: The more strongly tastiness was encoded in theta power early in the trial, the less strongly it was represented in the suppression of alpha power later in the trial.
source: In other words, the more strongly tastiness was encoded in theta power early in the trial, the less strongly it was represented in the suppression of alpha power later in the trial.
evidence: Inference drawn from the correlation between theta and alpha power changes

claim: The relationship between changes in alpha- and theta-correlates of tastiness was nonsignificant in the HEALTH condition.
source: This relationship was nonsignificant in the HEALTH condition (Pearson r = 0.12, p=0.39; Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing non-significant relationship, shown in Figure 5d

claim: Event-related potentials correlated with the time course of model-predicted taste-attribute signals, with no modulation by regulation.
source: Results suggested that event-related potentials (ERPs) correlated with the time course of model-predicted taste-attribute signals, with no modulation by regulation.
evidence: Summary of results from ERP analysis

claim: Suppression of frontal and occipital alpha power correlated with the time course of evidence accumulation, tracked tastiness according to its goal relevance, and predicted individual variation in successful down-regulation of tastiness.
source: By contrast, suppression of frontal and occipital alpha power correlated with the time course of EA, tracked tastiness according to its goal relevance, and predicted individual variation in successful down-regulation of tastiness.
evidence: Summary of results from alpha power analysis

claim: An earlier rise in frontal and occipital theta power represented food tastiness more strongly during regulation and predicted a weaker influence of food tastiness on behaviour.
source: Additionally, an earlier rise in frontal and occipital theta power represented food tastiness more strongly during regulation and predicted a weaker influence of food tastiness on behaviour.
evidence: Summary of results from theta power analysis

claim: Regulation modifies the representation of attributes during the process of evidence accumulation.
source: Our findings illuminate how regulation modifies the representation of attributes during the process of EA.
evidence: Overall conclusion drawn from the pattern of results

claim: Suppression of alpha oscillations reflects active information processing involving release from inhibition, perception, and attention and appears to be driven by cortico-cortical networks across frontal and parietal brain regions.
source: Suppression of alpha oscillations, also called the event-related desynchronization of alpha, is widely known to reflect active information processing involving release from inhibition, perception, and attention and appears to be driven by cortico-cortical networks across frontal and parietal brain regions (Foxe and Snyder, 2011; Klimesch, 2012; Klimesch et al., 2007; Samaha et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Foxe and Snyder, 2011; Klimesch, 2012; Klimesch et al., 2007; Samaha et al., 2018

claim: The degree of alpha suppression predicts success in tasks where a higher level of cortical excitation is required.
source: The degree of alpha suppression also predicts success in tasks where a higher level of cortical excitation is required (Klimesch et al., 2007), while inducing transient changes in alpha activity by external stimulation leads to predictable changes in cognitive performance (Klimesch et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klimesch et al., 2007 and Klimesch et al., 2003

claim: Prefrontal and posterior alpha suppression correlate with evidence accumulation in perceptual decision making.
source: Other work also supports the idea that prefrontal and posterior alpha suppression correlate with EA, although such studies have focused on perceptual decision making (Kloosterman et al., 2019; van Vugt et al., 2012; Werkle-Bergner et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kloosterman et al., 2019; van Vugt et al., 2012; Werkle-Bergner et al., 2014

claim: Alpha suppression may relate to the control of cortical excitability in relation to accumulation of sensory evidence.
source: This work suggests that alpha suppression may relate to the control of cortical excitability in relation to accumulation of sensory evidence (Kloosterman et al., 2019) in line with the proposed role for alpha in regulation of inhibition: increase in alpha power (synchronization) reflects inhibition and decrease in alpha power (desynchronization) reflects release from inhibition (Klimesch, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kloosterman et al., 2019 and Klimesch, 2012

claim: Tastier foods may typically result in release from inhibition, potentiating approach-related responding, but this process is disrupted during regulation.
source: One possibility, then, is that tastier foods may typically result in exactly this kind of release from inhibition, potentiating approach-related responding, but that this process is disrupted during regulation.
evidence: Speculation based on the pattern of alpha power results and known functions of alpha oscillations

claim: Theta oscillations in the frontal cortex reflect cognitive control and integration of resources for cognitive control.
source: Over the past several years, a consensus has emerged in the field that theta oscillations in the frontal cortex reflect cognitive control and integration of resources for cognitive control (e.g. Cavanagh and Frank, 2014; Mas-Herrero and Marco-Pallarés, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cavanagh and Frank, 2014; Mas-Herrero and Marco-Pallarés, 2016

claim: Midfrontal theta activates in response to any informative event or stimulus that conveys a need for behavioural adjustment or shift of attention.
source: Midfrontal theta, in particular, activates in response to any informative event or stimulus that conveys a need for behavioural adjustment or shift of attention (Cavanagh and Frank, 2014) and recruits regions underlying different cognitive operations to realize this need for control (Mas-Herrero and Marco-Pallarés, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cavanagh and Frank, 2014 and Mas-Herrero and Marco-Pallarés, 2016

claim: Posterior theta oscillations may reflect the encoding of new information by the hippocampus in several memory operations.
source: Posterior theta oscillations, on the other hand, may instead reflect the encoding of new information by the hippocampus in several memory operations (Axmacher et al., 2010; Klimesch, 1999; Scholz et al., 2017; Staudigl and Hanslmayr, 2013; Tesche and Karhu, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Axmacher et al., 2010; Klimesch, 1999; Scholz et al., 2017; Staudigl and Hanslmayr, 2013; Tesche and Karhu, 2000

claim: Early parietal and occipital theta oscillations correlate with value in high conflict choices and with cognitive load during mental calculation and multitasking.
source: There is scattered evidence that early parietal and occipital theta oscillations correlate with value in high conflict choices (Hunt et al., 2012) and with cognitive load during mental calculation and multitasking (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hunt et al., 2012 and Wang et al., 2018

claim: Frontal theta in value-based decisions shows sensitivity to emotional stimuli and efficient sensory integration.
source: On the other hand, frontal theta in value-based decisions also shows sensitivity to emotional stimuli and efficient sensory integration in different studies (Cavanagh et al., 2011; Nayak et al., 2019; Tosun et al., 2017; Zavala et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cavanagh et al., 2011; Nayak et al., 2019; Tosun et al., 2017; Zavala et al., 2016

claim: The theta-correlate of tastiness may represent an inhibitory control mechanism that helps to gate the impact of the constructed attribute and prevent it from integrating into the processes reflected by alpha at frontal and posterior sites.
source: This suggests that the theta-correlate of tastiness may represent an inhibitory control mechanism that helps to gate the impact of the constructed attribute that was reflected by front-central ERPS and prevent it from integrating into the processes reflected by alpha at frontal and posterior sites.
evidence: Speculation based on the pattern of theta power results and its relationship to alpha power

claim: Previous perceptual decision-making studies have found that ERPs, in particular the P300 at centro-parietal electrodes, reflect the evidence accumulation process predicted by drift-diffusion model.
source: While previous perceptual decision-making studies have found that ERPs, in particular the P300 at centro-parietal electrodes, reflect the EA process predicted by DDM (O'Connell et al., 2012; Twomey et al., 2015), our study found correlates of attribute values in ERPs with a more frontal distribution.
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Connell et al., 2012; Twomey et al., 2015

claim: This is the first report to suggest a differentiation in the computational functions reflected by ERP and oscillatory signals during value-based choice.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report to suggest a differentiation in the computational functions reflected by ERP and oscillatory signals during value-based choice, although such distinctions have been previously reported in other cognitive processes (Hajihosseini and Holroyd, 2013; Holroyd et al., 2012).
evidence: Claim of novelty with reference to related work in other cognitive processes

claim: Harris et al., 2013 reported an early attentional ERP component in occipital areas (N170) that was enhanced in successful self-control.
source: For example, Harris et al., 2013 reported an early attentional ERP component in occipital areas (N170) that was enhanced in successful self-control and later centro-parietal ERP components localized to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex that were sensitive to the overall value and tastiness and healthiness attributes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Harris et al., 2013

claim: The early EEG predictors of regulation observed in this study as well as in Harris et al., 2013 might indicate a common oscillatory mechanism (occipital theta power) that controls the processing of attributes in the service of regulation.
source: While a direct comparison of these two sets of findings is not possible due to differences in the study design and analysis, we speculate that the early EEG predictors of regulation observed in our study as well as in Harris et al., 2013 might indicate a common oscillatory mechanism (occipital theta power) that controls the processing of attributes in the service of regulation.
evidence: Speculation based on comparison with prior work

claim: The later components of attribute value represented by alpha suppression reflect the controlled integration of sensory evidence by areas involved in decision making and response selection.
source: We also speculate that the later components of attribute value represented by alpha suppression in our study reflect the controlled integration of sensory evidence by areas involved in decision making and response selection.
evidence: Speculation based on the pattern of alpha power results

claim: The study failed to replicate previous reports finding a distinct gamma (46–64 Hz) signature of value-based evidence accumulation at parietal and fronto-polar sites prior to response.
source: Importantly, while we do observe neural signatures consistent with EA signals in our study, our results fail to replicate some previous reports in the literature finding a distinct gamma (46–64 Hz) signature of value-based EA (Polanía et al., 2014) at parietal and fronto-polar sites prior to response.
evidence: Comparison with prior work showing non-replication

claim: The study did not find a significant increase in gamma power in relation to the pre-food baseline in either food-locked or response-locked analysis.
source: To test specifically whether we replicated this finding, we examined oscillatory power in the NATURAL condition averaged over all channels and specifically at Fz and Pz channels, but did not find an enhancement of gamma in relation to our pre-food 200 ms baseline (Figure 4—figure supplement 4a). To test whether this is due to higher variability in gamma phase in food-locked analysis, we also tested response-locked oscillatory power in relation to the pre-food baseline, but failed to find a significant increase in gamma power (Figure 4—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: Supported by analysis of gamma power shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: Discrepancies in gamma findings may be due to differences in the cognitive and memory demands presented by the different task paradigms.
source: We speculate that these discrepancies may be due to differences in the cognitive and memory demands presented by the different task paradigms.
evidence: Speculation about reasons for non-replication

claim: Polanía et al., 2014 found that fronto-central low-beta (18–20 Hz) power was negatively correlated with evidence accumulation.
source: In addition to gamma signals, Polanía et al., 2014 found that fronto-central low-beta (18–20 Hz) power was also negatively correlated with EA.
evidence: Supported by citation to Polanía et al., 2014

claim: The study observed suppression of low-beta power, though to a lesser degree compared to alpha power.
source: Similarly, we also observed suppression of low-beta power (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), though to a lesser degree compared to alpha power.
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: A full match to the single-trial value-based predictions of the drift-diffusion model regarding evidence accumulation only occurred with alpha suppression and did not match responses in the beta range.
source: A full match to the single-trial value-based predictions of our DDM model regarding EA only occurred with alpha suppression (Figure 4e, f) and did not match responses in the beta range.
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with alpha and beta power, shown in Figure 4e, f

claim: Regulation reduces the behavioural influence of tastiness not by disrupting early, stimulus-locked representations of tastiness, but by using a theta-related regulatory mechanism to disrupt the incorporation of tastiness into alpha-related evidence accumulation processes.
source: Taken together, our findings paint a nuanced portrait of the processes occurring during the regulation of value-based decision making. They suggest that regulation reduces the behavioural influence of tastiness not by disrupting early, stimulus-locked representations of tastiness, but by using a theta-related regulatory mechanism to disrupt the incorporation of tastiness into alpha-related EA processes.
evidence: Overall conclusion drawn from the pattern of results

claim: Alpha suppression may represent an identifiable signature indicating the integration of value-based attributes into the evidence accumulation process during both regulated and unregulated choices.
source: Our findings corroborate previous accounts suggesting that alpha suppression tracks EA and further suggest that alpha suppression may represent an identifiable signature indicating the integration of value-based attributes into the EA process during both regulated and unregulated choices.
evidence: Overall conclusion drawn from the pattern of results

claim: Theta oscillations might play a role in inhibiting the influence of attribute values on evidence accumulation, independent of regulation strategy.
source: Our study is also the first to our knowledge to find evidence that theta oscillations might play a role in inhibiting the influence of attribute values on EA, independent of regulation strategy.
evidence: Claim of novelty based on the pattern of theta power results

claim: 66 participants were recruited from the University of Toronto Scarborough research participation system and flyers posted on campus.
source: We recruited 66 participants from the University of Toronto Scarborough research participation system and flyers posted on campus.
evidence: Description of participant recruitment

claim: Five subjects did not complete the task either by choice or due to technical issues.
source: Five subjects did not complete the task either by choice or due to technical issues.
evidence: Description of participant exclusion

claim: Eleven subjects were excluded based on pre-registered exclusion criteria.
source: Eleven others were excluded based on our pre-registered exclusion criteria (more than three noisy channels in their EEG recording and/or if they made the same choice in more than 90% of trials in our NATURAL condition as described under Task [Open Science Framework; HajiHosseini and Hutcherson, 2020]).
evidence: Description of participant exclusion based on pre-registered criteria

claim: The final sample consisted of 50 usable subjects (30 females, age range 17–31).
source: Participants were recruited until we obtained our pre-registered target sample size of 50 usable subjects (HajiHosseini and Hutcherson, 2020; https://osf.io/ewtvx/; 30 females, age range 17–31).
evidence: Description of final sample size and demographics

claim: All participants were instructed to refrain from eating for 3 hr before the start of the experiment.
source: To increase motivation to eat, all participants were instructed to refrain from eating for 3 hr before the start of the experiment.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claim: The experiment consisted of three tasks: a pre-choice rating task, a self-regulation choice task (SRCT), and a post-choice rating task.
source: The experiment consisted of three tasks: a pre-choice rating task, a self-regulation choice task (SRCT), and a post-choice rating task (Hare et al., 2011; Harris et al., 2013; Hutcherson et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of experimental design with citations to similar prior work

claim: A 64-channel BioSemi ActiveTwo system was used for recording the EEG during the SRCT.
source: We used a 64-channel BioSemi ActiveTwo system for recording the EEG during the SRCT, aligned according to the 10-20 system.
evidence: Description of EEG recording equipment

claim: Recordings on Biosemi were sampled at 512 Hz, reference free, and later referenced to the averaged mastoids upon importing data to EEGLAB.
source: Recordings on Biosemi were sampled at 512 Hz, reference free, and later referenced to the averaged mastoids upon importing data to EEGLAB (Delorme and Makeig, 2004).
evidence: Description of EEG recording parameters with citation to EEGLAB

claim: The drift-diffusion model included six parameters per condition: weights on tastiness, healthiness, a constant, decision threshold, starting point bias, and non-decision time.
source: The DDM included six parameters per condition: three parameters related to drift rate (i.e. evidence/value formation) in each trial (weights on tastiness, wtastiness, healthiness, whealthiness, as well as a constant ValConst; total drift = wtastiness * tastiness + whealthiness * healthiness+ValConst), and three additional parameters: decision threshold (trs), starting point bias (spbias), and non-decision time (ndt) representing post-stimulus perceptual and pre-response motor processes.
evidence: Description of computational model structure

claim: HDDM uses hierarchical Bayesian estimation to identify the best-fitting parameters simultaneously for individual subjects and on the group level.
source: HDDM uses hierarchical Bayesian estimation to identify the best-fitting parameters simultaneously for individual subjects and on the group level, assuming individual subjects' parameters are drawn from the group distribution.
evidence: Description of model fitting procedure

claim: The average simulated posterior predictive response times were significantly correlated with the observed response times across subjects and conditions (mean r = 0.46).
source: We also found that the average simulated posterior predictive response times were significantly correlated with the observed response times across subjects and conditions (mean r = 0.46; t(49) = 17.1, p<0.001).
evidence: Model validation showing good fit to data
